correctness.rationale: The score bound u(d) <= c*d is strict at degrees 2 and 3; double counting n chosen 2-supported candidates gives exactly 2n incidences. Equality requires voter-degree 1 at all 2n vertices, a perfect matching. Every cubic bipartite graph has such a matching by Hall. The mapping is a bijection, graph-input recognition and matching-based winner verification are polynomial, and source #P-completeness of 3-regular bipartite perfect-matching counting is a published theorem. The standalone program verified 351,348 exact-rational score evaluations on 12 separate small graphs across four strict-sublinear score rules. Finite checks are supporting evidence, not a complexity proof.

originality.rationale: The primary 2026 counting theorem concerns unrestricted PAV and its construction uses high-support auxiliary voters; its conclusion calls for sparse-restriction classifications. The 2026 degree-two-support theorem solves finding a winner, not counting all optima. The 2023 graph-based reduction concerns greedy Thiele selection and does not logically imply the global-score maximizer bijection. The classical permanent hardness is credited as an input. The exact sparse counting classification was not found in the inspected sources, though an earlier implicit or explicit observation remains a plausible priority risk.

value.rationale: The 2026 literature specifically distinguishes finding one optimal sparse Thiele committee (polynomial) from counting all optima (not classified). The theorem gives a complete, parsimonious graph/election correspondence in a sparse regular domain, establishes #P-complete counting despite a known exact optimum and easy optimum construction, and applies to the full class of fixed rational scores with strictly sublinear second and third representations. This is a motivated computational boundary relevant to exact tie multiplicity, not a tiny numerical exercise. Simple proof does not make the counting-hardness classification trivial.
